stories.summary: Bangladesh lost around €1.82 billion in apparel exports to the EU in January–September 2026, its share falling to 19.06% from 21.10% a year earlier. Lower shipments, down 5.74%, and falling prices, down 6.54% to €13.70 per kg against an EU average of €19.59, caused the slide. China gained instead: its share rose to 34.29% on exports of €24.25 billion, up 4.46% — a core RMG, export and LDC-graduation question.

stories.headline: Bangladesh Bank decides to put Padma Bank under resolution
stories.summary: Bangladesh Bank has brought Padma Bank under its resolution framework, so the central bank will now decide whether to revive, merge or liquidate the troubled private lender. The decision came at the board meeting on Tuesday 17 November; the Bank Resolution Department will run the process and appoint an administrator, removing the existing board. Padma Bank, formerly The Farmers Bank, has struggled amid loan scandals — a live bank-resolution and governance case for BCS/Bank.

stories.exam_facts: Under the process, the administrator-led team will manage the bank's operations while the existing board of directors is removed; an external audit and an assessment of the bank's asset quality will then determine the next course; the specific approach has not yet been decided — once the department submits a proposal it will go to the board again, according to spokesperson Arief Hossain Khan; in early 2024 a memorandum of understanding was signed under Bangladesh Bank's facilitation to transfer Padma Bank's ownership to EXIM Bank, which itself has come under the control of the consolidated Islami Bank following the 2024 mass uprising; The Daily Star reports the decision was taken at a board meeting presided over by Governor Md Mostaqur Rahman.

stories.headline: Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
stories.summary: Myanmar faces a historic verdict at the International Court of Justice on Thursday 19 November in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia over the military's 2017 crackdown on the Rohingya. If The Gambia wins, it would be the first time an international court has found a state guilty of genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention. Hundreds of thousands fled to Bangladesh in August–September 2017 — a landmark international-law and Rohingya question.
stories.why_it_matters: A verdict for The Gambia would be the first time any international court has found a state guilty of genocide, and the 2017 expulsion that sent hundreds of thousands of Rohingya into Cox's Bazar is the background for every Bangladesh question on repatriation and international law.
stories.exam_facts: Since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948 following the Nazi Holocaust, individuals have been prosecuted for genocide in conflicts including Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia, but no state has ever been found guilty of the crime by an international court; Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar, said a verdict for The Gambia would give renewed importance to the 1948 Genocide Convention and international legal accountability for crimes committed by states; accounts of killings, torture and mass rape by Myanmar soldiers have been documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission; journalists witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages.

stories.headline: Enforced disappearance in Argentina and Bangladesh
stories.summary: Columnist Md Mahmudul Hasan argues enforced disappearance is carried out by state agents with their bosses' approval to silence dissent, hide atrocities and spread fear. He compares Argentina's Dirty War of 1976–1983, in which he writes up to 30,000 people fell victim, with Bangladesh, where he says victims have included civilians and military personnel. He describes Argentina's 'death flights' and a 1995 confession book — an opinion piece for human-rights and comparative-politics questions.
stories.why_it_matters: The columnist's comparison — Argentina's 30,000 Dirty War victims and 'death flights' against Bangladesh's civilian and military victims — gives the comparative frame for BCS/Bank questions on enforced disappearance and human rights.
stories.exam_facts: The columnist writes that after forcibly disappearing victims, state authorities deny holding them or knowing their whereabouts, and that requests for habeas corpus from victims' families are systematically overlooked; he writes that the Argentine military regime killed detainees through 'death flights', drugging prisoners and dropping them from helicopters or aircraft into the Atlantic Ocean, the Río de la Plata or other large water bodies; he writes that the atrocities were revealed in 1995 when Horacio Verbitsky's book El vuelo was published, its English version The Flight appearing in 1996, based on interviews with former naval officer Adolfo Scilingo, who confessed and called it 'a distasteful but necessary job'; citing Amnesty International, he writes enforced disappearance has taken place 'in many countries, in all regions of the world; from Mexico to Syria, from Bangladesh to Laos and from Bosnia and Herzegovina to Spain.'

stories.summary: Bangladesh Bank's board has approved a separate Tk30,000–40,000 crore Bank Resolution Fund to finance the restructuring, rescue and orderly liquidation of troubled banks and financial institutions.
